lesson.title: The Declaration of Independence's Core Principles
lesson.subject: social-studies

contentBlocks.text: We begin US History at its founding moment: 1776, when a document laid out the core principles the entire country would be built on.

The Declaration of Independence, adopted in 1776, established several core principles: that people have unalienable rights — life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness — that no government can rightfully take away; that governments get their power from the consent of the governed, not from a king's authority alone; and that people have the right to change or abolish a government that fails to protect their rights. These ideas were genuinely radical for their time, directly rejecting the idea that a monarch ruled by unquestionable right. Explain in your own words why 'government by consent of the governed' was such a different idea from how many governments worked before.
You just examined the core founding principles the United States was built on. Tomorrow we'll look at how the Constitution turned these principles into a real structure of government.

objectives: Identify the Declaration of Independence's core principles: unalienable rights, government by consent, right to alter government
Explain why 'government by consent of the governed' was a significant departure from prior forms of rule
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Introduce the Declaration of Independence and its 1776 context.
2. Walk through the three core principles: unalienable rights, consent of the governed, right to alter government.
3. Discuss why 'consent of the governed' was radical compared to monarchy.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's topic: the Constitution's structure of government.
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus on just 'unalienable rights' (life, liberty, pursuit of happiness) as the single clearest principle
Ready for more: ask them to think of a modern example where 'consent of the governed' shows up in how government works today (elections)

This week deliberately begins with founding principles and government structure — the tension between these ideals and the reality of slavery at the time is addressed in a later, more dedicated unit, not glossed over but also not compressed into this civics-structure lesson
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. Unalienable rights are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. 2. Government by consent means government gets its power from the people, not a king's unquestionable authority. 3. People have the right to change or abolish a government that fails to protect their rights.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Establishes the C3 Framework Civics dimension's foundational document before the course moves into government structure and, in future units, the war and its consequences — matching the course's own 'founding era' starting point.
